dataset_family: CIMA-Q (Consortium for the Early Identification of Alzheimer's Disease - Quebec): recruited from the NuAge cohort, memory clinics and the community in Montreal, Quebec City and Sherbrooke; 140 SCD at T1, 80 reassessed at 4 years (21 progressed to MCI/AD, 59 did not)
method_family: Small prospective research-cohort comparison: baseline Mann-Whitney U and chi-square tests of GDS-30 total, presence (>= 3 items) and Adams subdimensions (and GAI) between SCD progressors and non-progressors; no multivariable model beyond an age-adjusted re-run described in words; no brain measures
what_it_shows: Among 80 older adults with subjective cognitive decline followed for 4 years in CIMA-Q (21 progressed to NIA-AA MCI or probable AD, 59 did not; 43% attrition from 140), baseline GDS-30 total did not differ between progressors and non-progressors (7.43 +/- 6.66 vs 5.46 +/- 4.91; Mann-Whitney U 517.5, p = 0.263), and neither did the proportion endorsing 3 or more items (71.4% vs 66.1%, p = 0.654). Only the hopelessness dimension (p = 0.048) and the powerlessness item (p = 0.009) were higher in progressors, uncorrected. Clinical depression was an exclusion criterion. No brain measure.
why: Raymond-Lessard, Belanger, Hudon, Grenier and the CIMA-Q Group, J Alzheimers Dis 104(3) (2025) 720-731, DOI 10.1177/13872877251319538. The summaries.md block is headed by the PDF filename and has no author list, but it describes this study (CIMA-Q, GAI and GDS-30, 140 at baseline, 21/59 at follow-up), and the map DOI matches the PDF. Against the Table A1 statement: the study's own continuous-severity comparison is null for progression, which resembles the conversion limb ('continuous severity scores fail to track ... conversion'). But it is on a different population and a different outcome. The participants have SCD, not MCI, and the outcome is progression from SCD to MCI or AD, not MCI-to-dementia conversion. The row is about 'MCI neurobiology and prognosis', so under the brief's different-population rule this is 'partly' at most. The part shown: in cognitively unimpaired older adults with SCD, baseline depressive-symptom intensity on the GDS-30 did not separate those who developed MCI or AD within 4 years. Further limits: 21 progressors, and the authors themselves flag type II error; clinical depression was excluded, so the range is subclinical (mean about 6 of 30); univariate Mann-Whitney tests only; the hopelessness difference is one of six uncorrected subscale tests. The study cuts slightly against the first clause: screen-level depressive symptoms (GDS >= 3) were no more common in those who developed MCI or AD. With clinical depression excluded, though, this is not a test of depression status. Reporting defects that do not touch the GDS total row: the intensity result prints z = -1.20 with p = 0.263, although a two-tailed z of 1.20 gives about 0.23; Table 1's women counts (14 and 47) sum to 61, but the total is printed as 58 (72.5%) and the text says 58%; Table 2's anxiety-subdimension SD '.14' looks like a typo. Independence: CIMA-Q (Montreal, Quebec City, Sherbrooke; partly recruited from NuAge) is not the dataset of any current supporter or of any round-1 or round-2 candidate, and no authors are shared. Not a preprint. Quotes are transliterated to ASCII (+/- for the plus-minus sign, x2 for chi-square as printed in the extract, - for the minus sign).

quotes.quote: The presence, type and intensity of anxiety symptoms did not significantly distinguish the two groups. Only one type of hopelessness-related depressive symptom was significantly higher in SCD participants who had progressed to objective cognitive decline compared with those who had not.

Respondents were also excluded if they had too-advanced dementia or if they had a clinical physical or psychological condition, such as clinical depression or an anxiety disorder, that could better explain their scores on questionnaires and scales measuring their cognitive state.
These participants also had to meet NIA-AA diagnostic criteria for MCI48 or probable AD49 at follow-up.
From the initial sample, 80 were reassessed at time 2 (T2). The 4-year attrition rate was 43%
Among the 80 participants with SCD, 21 individuals progressed to objective cognitive losses (SCD-P) either to MCI or AD, and 59 did not develop any (SCD-NP).

Concerning the presence of depressive symptoms, our analyses showed that 66.1% of SCD-NP individuals endorsed three or more items on the GDS compared to 71.4% of SCD-P individuals at T1 of the study. The relationship between cognitive decline and report of depressive symptoms was found to be non-significant x2(1; N = 80) = 0.200, p = 0.654.
Concerning the type of symptoms, the hopelessness dimension was significatively higher in the SCD-P group, U(N of SCD-P = 21; N of SCD-NP = 59) = 457.5, z = -1.977, p = 0.048.
Regarding the intensity of depressive symptoms, it was not significant, U(N of SCD-P = 21; N of SCD-NP = 59) = 517.5, z = -1.20, p = 0.263.
We did not find that a greater intensity of self-reported depressive symptoms was manifested in individuals with SCD who developed objective cognitive losses after 4 years

The lack of significance might also be explained by the relatively small size of the sample compared to other studies carried out in the same field. This could have increased the risk of a type II error.
As age tended to become significant, we re-run the analyses with age as a covariate; results remained not statistically significant.
